582.title: Bring us back
582.hook: the next asks for return to the Torah and to God
582.carry: the way back was already built in
582.howItsDone: Hashiveinu, the request for return, is the fifth blessing of the weekday Amidah; the verse from Lamentations it echoes is also sung as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, binah, the first thing the Amidah asks for. Your line was an understanding heart. Did you ask one more question before deciding? Today, what understanding leads to. Day five hundred eighty-two.

A phone's map app has one phrase it says more patiently than any person ever could. Rerouting. You missed the exit, you took the wrong lane, you ignored it three times in a row. It never says you idiot. It never says go home. It just quietly works out the way back from exactly where you are. The second request of the Amidah is built on the same idea. Once you understand where you are, the next thing to ask for is the way back.
screen: `REROUTING.` → `NEVER: YOU IDIOT.` → `THE WAY BACK FROM WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: The fifth blessing says: bring us back, our Father, to Your Torah. Draw us near, our King, to Your service. And return us in complete teshuvah before You. Blessed are You, who desires teshuvah. Teshuvah is usually translated repentance, but it shares its verb with turning, returning: the same verb as in the Lamentations verse. It's less about feeling terrible and more about changing direction. The blessing echoes the end of the book of Lamentations. In the old Jewish translation: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned." Notice the grammar. The person praying asks God to do the turning. It admits that coming back is hard to do alone. Notice the two names too. First our Father, then our King. The close relationship comes first, then the formal one. Why does this come right after understanding? The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, points to a verse in Isaiah that runs understanding with their heart, return, and be healed, to explain why return comes right after understanding. You can't turn around until you see where you are. And the blessing's ending is gentle: God desires teshuvah. Wants it. Elsewhere the Talmud, in Pesachim 54a, lists teshuvah among seven things created before the world itself. Before anyone could go wrong, the way back was already built in.
screen: `TESHUVAH: TURNING, RETURNING.` · `TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.` · `FIRST FATHER, THEN KING.` · `UNDERSTAND, THEN RETURN.` · then, large: `BRING US BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn back one step. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you've drifted from who you meant to be. A habit that slipped. A friendship you let go quiet. A promise to yourself you stopped keeping. Don't make a plan for the whole road. Just picture the first step back: one text, one page, one walk, one honest sentence. Notice that you can take it from exactly where you are. If you pray, you can ask for help turning. The bell holds the time.
Teshuvah. Return, turning around — what the Amidah's fifth blessing asks God to bring us back to, a way back God desires and already built in.
Your line: the way back was already built in. Today, take the one step back you pictured, and keep it small enough that you actually take it. Day five hundred eighty-two.

583.title: Forgive us
583.hook: a gentle tap on the chest as forgiveness is asked
583.carry: easier when you don't let it build up
583.howItsDone: Selach lanu is the sixth blessing of the weekday Amidah; many Jews lightly strike the left side of the chest with the right fist at the words chatanu and pashanu.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the request to turn around. Your line was the way back was already built in. Did you take one small step back? Today, the next request, and a small motion of the hand. Day five hundred eighty-three.
screen: `THE WAY BACK WAS ALREADY BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: Three times a day, on weekdays, in the middle of a silent prayer, people's right hands come up and touch their chests. Not a punch. Not a dramatic gesture. Two light taps with a loose fist, over the heart, so small you'd miss it from across the room. Then the hand goes down, and the prayer goes on. It happens on two words. And they're two words people find hard to say, even in a whisper.
screen: `A HAND COMES UP TO THE CHEST.` → `TWO LIGHT TAPS OVER THE HEART.` → `TWO HARD WORDS.`

segments.voice: The sixth blessing says: forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned. Pardon us, our King, for we have transgressed. For You pardon and forgive. Blessed are You, gracious One, who forgives abundantly. The two words are chatanu, we have sinned, and pashanu, we have transgressed. At each one, many people tap their chest. The custom is often explained this way: the heart is where wanting starts, so that's where you knock. Notice that it's we, not I. Even alone, you pray in the plural. The word for forgiveness here is selichah. Some readers note that in the Hebrew Bible, the verb behind it, salach, is used of God doing the forgiving. When Moses pleads for the people after the spies, God answers, in the old Jewish translation: "I have pardoned according to thy word." Jews hear that line again every year on the night of Yom Kippur. And the blessing's ending, who forgives abundantly, echoes Isaiah: let the wicked return to God, "for He will abundantly pardon." The Talmud's order makes sense now. Understanding, then return, then forgiveness. You see what you did, you turn around, and then you ask to be let go of it. And it's said every weekday, not once a year. Forgiveness in the Amidah isn't a dramatic event. It's maintenance, like brushing your teeth: small, daily, and much easier when you don't let it build up.
screen: `WE HAVE SINNED. WE HAVE TRANSGRESSED.` · `A TAP WHERE WANTING STARTS.` · `SELICHAH: GOD'S FORGIVING.` · `UNDERSTAND, RETURN, BE FORGIVEN.` · then, large: `FORGIVE US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tap your heart for one wrong. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Find one thing you did that you wish you hadn't. Not the worst thing in your life. Just one real, recent thing: a sharp word, a corner cut, a person ignored. Name it to yourself, honestly. Then, if you like, tap your chest once, gently. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven. Then let your hand rest, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Selichah. Forgiveness. The Amidah's sixth blessing, asked in the plural, with a tap over the heart.
Your line: easier when you don't let it build up. Today, if the wrong you named involved another person, say sorry to them, in one plain sentence. Day five hundred eighty-three.

584.title: See our trouble
584.hook: look upon our affliction and redeem us
584.howItsDone: Re'eh ve'onyenu is the seventh blessing of the weekday Amidah, ending go'el Yisrael; on public fast days the leader adds the prayer Aneinu between this blessing and the next.

segments.voice: Yesterday, selichah, a tap over the heart. Your line was easier when you don't let it build up. Did you say one plain sorry? Today, the request that comes right after forgiveness: the request to be seen. Day five hundred eighty-four.
screen: `EASIER WHEN YOU DON'T LET IT BUILD UP.`

segments.voice: There's a particular kind of loneliness in trouble nobody notices. The rent that's late again. The marriage that looks fine from the outside. The test results you haven't told anyone about. Often, before we want anyone to fix it, we want someone to see it. A friend who says, that sounds really hard, can matter more than one who rushes to solutions. The seventh blessing of the Amidah opens with exactly that request. Before rescue, before redemption: look.
screen: `TROUBLE NOBODY NOTICES.` → `BEFORE FIXING, SEEING.` → `THE SEVENTH BLESSING: LOOK.`

segments.voice: The seventh blessing says: look upon our affliction, and fight our fight, and redeem us quickly, for Your name's sake, for You are a mighty redeemer. Blessed are You, Redeemer of Israel. In Hebrew it opens re'eh ve'onyenu: see our affliction. That word for affliction, oni, takes us back to the burning bush. There God says to Moses, in the old Jewish translation: "I have surely seen the affliction of My people." Same word. The Exodus starts with God seeing. So the blessing asks God to do again what began the first redemption. Fight our fight is a phrase from the Psalms: take up our case, be on our side in the quarrel. You may remember another word here: go'el, the redeemer who buys back. Before the Amidah, the Shema's blessing ended ga'al Yisrael, who redeemed, in the past. Here it's go'el Yisrael, who redeems, now. The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, says this blessing is seventh because redemption is expected in a seventh year. And the commentator Rashi adds that it isn't about the great final redemption, which comes later in the Amidah. It's about the daily troubles that keep coming. On public fast days, the leader adds a short extra prayer right after this blessing, aneinu: answer us. The blessing doesn't ask for trouble to vanish. It asks, first, that it be seen, and then that someone take our side.
screen: `RE'EH VE'ONYENU: SEE OUR AFFLICTION.` · `I HAVE SURELY SEEN, AT THE BUSH.` · `GA'AL: REDEEMED. GO'EL: REDEEMS.` · `FOR THE TROUBLES THAT KEEP COMING.` · then, large: `SEE OUR TROUBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one affliction honestly. Settle, and breathe. Find one trouble you're carrying right now, the one you usually describe as fine. Name it plainly, in a short sentence, without softening it and without making it bigger. Just true. If you pray, you can say it as a request to be seen: look at this. If you don't, let yourself be the one who sees it, and stay with it for a few breaths instead of looking away. The bell holds the time.
Oni. Affliction — the word from the burning bush, where God saw it, now asked again in the Amidah: see our affliction, and fight our fight.
Your line: I hear you. Today, when someone tells you about a hard thing, see it before you try to fix it: one sentence that says I hear you. Day five hundred eighty-four.

585.title: Heal us
585.hook: names of the sick are added here in many communities
585.howItsDone: Refa'enu is the eighth blessing of the weekday Amidah; many Jews add a personal prayer for someone who is ill within it, naming the person by their Hebrew name and their mother's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the request to be seen in trouble. Your line was I hear you. Did you hear someone before trying to fix it? Today, the eighth blessing, where people bring names. Day five hundred eighty-five.

Stand near someone saying the silent Amidah and, at one point, you might catch a pause. A longer one than usual. Their lips keep moving, but not with the printed words. If you could hear, you'd hear names. Sarah, daughter of Miriam. David, son of Ruth. A grandmother in the hospital. A friend's child in chemo. A coworker they barely know. The prayer book leaves a door open here, right in the middle of the prayer's fixed words.
screen: `A LONGER PAUSE.` → `NAMES, NOT PRINTED WORDS.` → `A DOOR LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: The eighth blessing begins with a verse from the prophet Jeremiah, who prays, in the old Jewish translation: "Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved; for Thou art my praise." The Amidah takes Jeremiah's words and changes one thing. Me becomes us. Heal us, and we shall be healed. Even about illness, the prayer speaks as a group. Then it asks for refuah shleimah, complete healing, for all our wounds, and ends: blessed are You, who heals the sick of Your people Israel. Refuah is healing; a rofe is a doctor, and you heard the same root in Gevurot, God heals the sick. The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, explains why healing is eighth: circumcision happens on the eighth day, and the baby needs healing after it. And in Avodah Zarah 8a, it says that a person with someone sick at home may mention them in this blessing. So in many communities, people add names here, quietly. A common custom is to use the person's Hebrew name and their mother's name: David son of Ruth. Some say the phrase refuah shleimah, complete healing, of body and of spirit. Notice the order of the whole run of requests. Understanding, return, forgiveness, being seen, then healing. The body gets its turn right after the heart, and it gets it every day.
screen: `JEREMIAH: HEAL ME.` · `THE AMIDAH: HEAL US.` · `REFUAH SHLEIMAH: COMPLETE HEALING.` · `NAMES ADDED, WITH A MOTHER'S NAME.` · then, large: `HEAL US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add one name to your prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's sick right now, in body or in spirit. It might be someone close, or someone you only heard about. Picture their face if you can. Then say their name, quietly. If you know their mother's name, you can add it, the way many Jews do. If you pray, you can ask for their complete healing. If not, simply hold the name with care for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Refuah. Healing. The Amidah's eighth blessing, Jeremiah's prayer made plural, where names of the sick are added.
Your line: thinking of you. Today, send one short message to the person whose name you held: thinking of you. Day five hundred eighty-five.

586.title: Bless the year
586.hook: a prayer for the year's harvest and livelihood
586.howItsDone: Birkat hashanim is the ninth blessing of the weekday Amidah; Jews in Israel add the request for dew and rain from the seventh of Cheshvan, Jews elsewhere from early December, and some add personal requests for livelihood within it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, refuah, healing, with names added quietly. Your line was thinking of you. Did you send that message? Today, the ninth blessing, about money, food and work. Day five hundred eighty-six.

Here's a strange fact about Jewish prayer outside the land of Israel. On a date in early December, Jews in New York, London and Buenos Aires change one line of the weekday Amidah. Not on a Jewish holiday. On a date tied to an old way of counting from the autumn equinox. In Israel the change comes weeks earlier. The line is about rain. But it sits inside a blessing about something everyone, everywhere, worries about: making a living.
screen: `A LINE CHANGES IN EARLY DECEMBER.` → `NOT ON A JEWISH HOLIDAY.` → `A BLESSING ABOUT MAKING A LIVING.`

segments.voice: The ninth blessing is called birkat hashanim, the blessing of the years. It says: bless this year for us, and all its kinds of produce, for good. Satisfy us from its goodness, and bless our year like the good years. Blessed are You, who blesses the years. In the rainy season, people ask: give dew and rain for a blessing. In the dry season, simply: give blessing. A week ago we met the rain line in Gevurot. That one praises God who makes the rain fall. This one actually asks for it. In Israel, the asking begins in the autumn, on the seventh of the month of Cheshvan; the Mishnah explains the delay: so that the last pilgrim from the festival could get home, as far as the river Euphrates, before the rain. Outside Israel, Jews follow the Babylonian Talmud's reckoning, which is why the date lands in early December. The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, also has a sharp reason for why this blessing is ninth: against people who drive prices up, because of a line in what it counts as the ninth psalm, break the arm of the wicked. Even a blessing about harvests keeps one eye on fairness. If you don't farm, the blessing still fits. Some add their own words here about work and income, what Jews call parnassah, livelihood. Like the good years: a modest request. Not a fortune. A year that feeds you, the way the good ones did.
screen: `BIRKAT HASHANIM: BLESS THE YEARS.` · `ASKING FOR RAIN, NOT ONLY PRAISING.` · `ISRAEL IN AUTUMN, ABROAD IN DECEMBER.` · `PARNASSAH: A LIVING.` · then, large: `BLESS THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless your work this year. Settle, and breathe. Picture your work, whatever it is: a job, a business, school, caring for kids or parents, looking for work. Picture the year ahead of it, the good months and the slow ones. Now hold one modest hope for it: not a windfall, just a year that feeds you and the people who depend on you. If you pray, you can ask for that in the words of the blessing, like the good years. The bell holds the time.
Parnassah. Livelihood — what the ninth blessing, birkat hashanim, asks for alongside rain and harvest: a year that feeds you, like the good years.
Your line: a year that feeds you. Today, do one piece of your work with care, as if it were a seed for the year. Day five hundred eighty-six.

587.title: Gather the scattered
587.hook: sound the great shofar for freedom and gather the scattered
587.howItsDone: Teka beshofar, the request to gather the exiles, is the tenth blessing of the weekday Amidah, said three times a day; communities differ in how they relate it to the modern State of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing of the years. Your line was a year that feeds you. Did one piece of work get done with care? Today, the Amidah turns from the private to the whole people. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Pull up a map of where Jewish families have lived. Babylon and Baghdad. Cordoba and Toledo. Fez, Cairo, Aleppo, Sana'a. Vilna, Kraków, Odessa. Cochin on the coast of India. Then Brooklyn, Buenos Aires, Johannesburg, Melbourne. One Shabbat table can hold a recipe from Aleppo and a lullaby from Vilna. Some families carry two or three of those names in their own story. In all of those places, every weekday, the same line of the Amidah has spoken directly to that map.
screen: `BABYLON, CORDOBA, FEZ, VILNA.` → `COCHIN, BROOKLYN, BUENOS AIRES.` → `A LINE THAT SPEAKS TO THE MAP.`

segments.voice: The tenth blessing says: sound the great shofar for our freedom. Raise a banner to gather our exiles, and gather us together from the four corners of the earth. Blessed are You, who gathers the dispersed of Your people Israel. The great shofar comes from the prophet Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation: "it shall come to pass in that day, that a great horn shall be blown," and the lost and the scattered come home to worship in Jerusalem. The banner comes from Isaiah too: a signal raised high, so people far away can see where to come. Notice the first word of the blessing is not gather. It's teka: blow. The shofar is the sound of the Jubilee year, when slaves went free and land returned to its families. So freedom comes first, then gathering. Here the requests turn toward the whole people's future, from my troubles to our story. The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, says it follows the blessing of the years because a prophet promised that when the land bears fruit again, the exiles will be near. Jews have said these words in Baghdad and Vilna and Cochin, far from Jerusalem. In modern times, some see the return of Jews to the land of Israel in this light, and others read the blessing as pointing to a future not yet here. Either way, every weekday, scattered people ask to be gathered.
screen: `TEKA: BLOW THE GREAT SHOFAR.` · `RAISE A BANNER FOR THE EXILES.` · `FREEDOM FIRST, THEN GATHERING.` · `FROM MY TROUBLES TO OUR STORY.` · then, large: `GATHER THE SCATTERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone far away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love who lives far from you: a sibling across the country, a grandparent in another land, a friend who moved and slowly went quiet. Picture where they are right now, what time it is there, what they might be doing. Imagine, for a moment, the whole table together again. If you pray, you can hold them in this blessing. The bell holds the time.
Teka. Blow: the Amidah's tenth blessing opens with the shofar's blast, then asks to gather the exiles from the four corners of the earth.
Your line: freedom comes first, then gathering. Today, reach out to the far-away person you pictured, and make one plan, however small, to be in the same place. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

588.title: Restore justice
588.hook: restore our judges as at first
588.carry: kindness and justice, from the same throne
588.howItsDone: Hashivah shofteinu is the eleventh blessing of the weekday Amidah; during the Ten Days of Repentance its closing changes from the King who loves righteousness and justice to the King of judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great shofar and the scattered people. Your line was freedom comes first, then gathering. Did you make a plan with someone far away? Today, once the people are gathered, the question of who judges them. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

A landlord who ignored the law. A boss who promoted the friend. A court case that dragged on for years and ended up with the side that had more money. A referee who never saw the foul. The trouble is not just that something went wrong. It is that the place you were supposed to go when things go wrong was broken too. The eleventh blessing of the Amidah is a prayer about exactly that place.
screen: `A SYSTEM THAT DIDN'T WORK.` → `THE PLACE YOU GO, BROKEN TOO.` → `THE ELEVENTH BLESSING.`

segments.voice: It says: restore our judges as at first, and our counselors as at the beginning. Remove from us sorrow and sighing. Reign over us, You alone, with kindness and compassion, and vindicate us in judgment. Blessed are You, King who loves righteousness and justice. The first line is lifted almost word for word from Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation: "And I will restore thy judges as at the first, and thy counsellors as at the beginning." Isaiah is speaking to a Jerusalem whose leaders, he says, love bribes and ignore the orphan and the widow. The repair he imagines isn't a new system. It's a return to the old one working the way it should. Some readers hear in as at first the Torah's picture of judges: when Moses is worn out from judging everyone himself, his father-in-law Jethro tells him to find capable people, who fear God, who love truth and hate unjust gain. Notice what sits inside a blessing about justice: kindness and compassion. The blessing doesn't set justice and mercy against each other. It asks for both from the same throne. It ends with two words a psalm also pairs, saying God loves righteousness and justice: tzedakah and mishpat. And during the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, the ending changes to the King of judgment, because tradition holds that this is the season when God judges the world. For ten days, the ending names God as the judge.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for fair leaders. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who make decisions over your life: a judge, a mayor, a principal, a manager, a landlord, a referee. Pick one. Picture them on an ordinary day, with a hard decision on their desk. Hold one wish for them: that they see clearly, that they can't be bought, that they're kind to the person with the least power in the room. If you pray, you can ask it. The bell holds the time.
Restore justice. Hashivah shofteinu. The Amidah's eleventh blessing: return our judges as at first, with kindness and compassion.

Your line: kindness and justice, from the same throne. A week of requests: bring us back, forgive us, see our trouble, heal us, bless the year, freedom comes first, then gathering, and now fair judges. Today, in one small decision you make about someone else, be the fair judge. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

myth: the blessing sets justice against mercy
it asks God to reign with kindness and compassion, and to judge justly.
the blessing's ending changes between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
it becomes the King of judgment for those ten days.
Isaiah imagines a brand-new system of courts
he imagines judges as at the first: the old system working as it should.

fork.setup: you're Moses. people line up from morning to evening for you to judge every case. what does Jethro tell you to do?
options: keep going; only you can do it.
find capable, honest people who hate unjust gain to judge with you.
fork.reveal: Jethro tells him to share the work with capable people who fear God, love truth and hate unjust gain.

original.note: Hebrew: restore our judges. the opening of the eleventh blessing, from Isaiah 1:26.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer about ancient courts.
what it means: a prayer for the places we go when things go wrong to work fairly, with kindness and compassion.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 1:26 adapted; Exodus 18:21 behind as at first; hamelech hamishpat in the Ten Days of Repentance (Berakhot 12b).
